p: On the Sunday of the March drill, after Vern told Kit she'd sat the test before, she went back to the dark shop, lifted the foam in her toolbox lid, and took out her 2019 score sheet. From then on it rode in her coat.

At three in the morning at the water plant, the chlorine feed pump lost its prime. Kit bled the gas out of the pump head, read the night's log to see when it had quit, and worked the pounds of chlorine with the plant's formula. The night lead, Leon Yates, asked her to leave it out of the log. It was the third time that month, and he'd kept the first two out himself. She told him to his face she was writing hers, and that his two nights went in the book before the supervisor read it at seven, or she'd tell him she knew. He wrote them before the morning huddle. Driving to Vern's the next night, she thought about how long she'd been leaving one out of her own book.

On Tuesday at Vern's kitchen table she said it plain. In 2019 her Pilot score came back nineteen, and the minimum is twenty five. Boyd had asked her to stay that winter, and she'd said yes because yes was easier than saying nineteen out loud. Then she'd let the shop, her mother, Graham and Boyd himself think it was Boyd, for seven years.

Vern told her about 1973, when he failed the flight physical's eye chart by one line and took the navigator's seat instead. He printed the word from his form, ACUITY, in the margin under her nineteen, the first writing anyone had put on that page. He told her about thirty one years as a freight dispatcher in Kansas City. She gave him the sentence from her letter on an index card, I want to fly, and he stood it against his percolator. Then he showed her an old log where a crew chief grounded a jet his own fuel math said could fly, and she saw that for seven years she'd let a nineteen answer a question nobody had asked her.

That night she told Graham there was a part of 2019 he hadn't heard, that it was hers and not Boyd's, and that she'd tell him all of it on Saturday, April 3, after the practice test. She heard herself say after. He wrote 2019 on the whiteboard in that Saturday's square.

Vern's wife, Patrice, sent Kit home with a gooseberry pie and told her he hadn't talked this much in years. On Saturday in the heritage room Kit asked Vern to keep it until she'd told Graham and Boyd herself. He said he could ask. He said it wasn't his to tell, and it wasn't hers to keep forever. Then, though it was a Saturday and logs came on Tuesdays, he handed her one folded once, and she took it home without opening it.
Corbin Haas. Tech sergeant in the avionics shop, back from chapter two. Two years ago the wing sent him to pilot training, and he washed out and came home to the shop.

Sunday, March 21, a little after five in the morning. Kit had slept four hours and come awake the way the plant had trained her to, all at once, with no reason she could name. Graham was still asleep upstairs. She made coffee in the dark and sat down at the kitchen table in her coat.

The log was in the inside pocket, folded once, on top of the other sheet. It had ridden home on the passenger seat the afternoon before and spent the night in her coat on the hook by the door. Vern gave her logs on Tuesdays, at the end of the night, picked for whatever they'd worked on that week. She'd gone to the heritage room about 2019, and he'd told her it wasn't his to tell and it wasn't hers to keep forever. Then he'd dug in his jacket and handed her this, and he hadn't said what it was for.
She unfolded it under the light over the stove.

My log, nineteen March, oh one. Northbound to the track. Doppler quit at fourteen ten Zulu. True airspeed five hundred. Wind two seven zero at one forty, straight across the course. Drew it on the chart. Steered three four four. Ground speed four eighty. Made good three six zero. Rendezvous on time. Pointed it sixteen left to go straight.
She read it twice. The second time she only read the last line.

She knew crab from the ramp, from watching them come down final on a windy day with the nose pointed off the runway. He'd pointed the nose into the thing pushing him, because that was the only way to go straight. She'd spent seven years pointing away from hers and calling the drift the wing.
The Doppler on that airplane quit on me three times in 2001. Each time I had a chart, a grease pencil, and whatever arithmetic I'd carried up there in my head. Bring yours the same way.

Math Knowledge comes fourth, right after Word Knowledge. The current Pearson page gives it 25 problems in 22 minutes. Call it fifty three seconds each, and they don't come out even. The 2015 practice pamphlet says five choices apiece, and it was written for a paper booklet with scratch paper handed out. What a computer test center gives you to write on, I can't promise you, so practice on plain paper and count on nothing fancier. I can't tell you for certain whether there's a calculator on the screen either, so practice like there isn't one.

It's the math bare, no word problems: arithmetic, the names of things, algebra, and geometry. You saw it all in school. When the algebra's slow, plug in the answers, one at a time, and see which fits. A wrong answer costs no more than a blank, and Pearson won't score you until every item has an answer, so put your best guess on a slow one and go. I've watched people spend four of those minutes on one circle.
How the exam asks it. Take the quick ones quick. A definition's worth ten seconds of your clock, not forty, and you'll want the change for a circle.

Start with the names, because that's where the cheap points are, and I hate to watch anybody leave cheap points on the table. Prime first. A prime has exactly two factors, itself and 1, so 1 doesn't make it, and 2's the only even one that does. The sneaky ones look prime and aren't. Patrice's sister lived at 91 Cedar for thirty years, and I never drove past that mailbox without thinking seven thirteens. Fifty one's another, three seventeens. Try 3 and try 7 before you call anything prime.

A factor goes into a number, and a multiple is what you get counting by it. Take 18 and 30. Six is the biggest thing that goes into both, so that's the greatest common factor. Ninety's the smallest number they both go into, the least common multiple. I find that one the lazy way, counting up by the bigger number till the smaller one fits, 30, 60, 90, and I've never found a faster way I trusted. Folks mix those two up constantly, and both often sit in the choices.

Integers are the whole numbers with their negatives and zero thrown in: minus 4, 0, 17. Nothing with a decimal point in it. A rational number is anything you can write as one integer over another, and that's a bigger crowd than it sounds. 0.75 is rational, it's three fourths. Minus 6 is rational. A decimal that repeats forever is too, since 0.333 and on and on is one third. Irrational ones never come out as a fraction of integers: pi, and the root of anything that isn't a perfect square, like root 2 or root 12. I'll tell you the miss I see most. Somebody calls root 16 irrational because it's wearing a root sign. It's 4.

A factorial is a whole number times every whole number under it, down to 1, and it's written with an exclamation point, like the number's hollering at you. Five factorial is 5 times 4 times 3 times 2 times 1. That's 120. When one sits over another, cancel what they share, and seven factorial over five factorial comes down to 7 times 6, 42. People take 7 minus 5, get 2, and go hunting for 2 factorial. Factorials don't subtract. I never needed one in an airplane, and I'd still rather you had it in your pocket.

Absolute value is distance from zero, so it's never negative. Call it miles from the field. Nobody's ever minus six miles out, though I've flown with a few who acted like it. Work inside the bars first: the absolute value of 3 minus 11 is 8. A reciprocal flips a fraction over, two sevenths to seven halves, and times the original it makes 1. The reciprocal of minus 5 is minus one fifth, and I'd underline that the sign stays put. Changing the sign is the opposite, a different word, and the test likes to offer both. A coefficient is the number stuck on a letter, the 4 in 4x.
Try one. The greatest common factor and least common multiple of 8 and 12 are 4 and 24. If you said 96, you multiplied them. That's a common multiple all right, just not the least one.
How the exam asks it. When two choices are a factor and a multiple, or a reciprocal and an opposite, read the question's word again before you pick.
Dispatch ran on fractions. Three quarters of a tank, two thirds of a crew day. If you can't add those in your head, you'll be asking somebody else, and they'll be busy.

To add or subtract fractions, the bottoms have to match first. I never liked that rule and I never found a way around it. Say a drum's three eighths full and you pour in five twelfths of a drum. Count by 12 till 8 fits, 12, 24, the least common multiple from the last page. Three eighths is nine twenty fourths, top and bottom times 3. Five twelfths is ten twenty fourths. Add the tops, keep the bottom: nineteen twenty fourths. The miss is adding straight across, 3 and 5 over 8 and 12, eight twentieths. That's two fifths, less than the five twelfths you poured in, and a drum doesn't get emptier from pouring. Subtracting's the same. Bottoms first.

Multiplying's the easy one, and I take easy where I find it, same as anybody who's flown nights. Tops times tops, bottoms times bottoms. Cancel first if you can. Two thirds times nine tenths: 2 into 10 is 5, 3 into 9 is 3, and you're holding three fifths without ever having seen a big number. I like it when I never see a big number. Dividing, you flip the second one and multiply. Flip the second, never the first, and I'd say that out loud at the table. Three fourths divided by three eighths is three fourths times eight thirds. That's 2. Flip the wrong one and you get a half, and they put a half in the choices for you. Sense check: two cans of three eighths fill three fourths. Two.

Mixed numbers, like 2 and a half, get made into one fraction before you multiply or divide. No exceptions I ever found. Two and a half, five halves. One and a third, four thirds. Five halves times four thirds is twenty sixths, ten thirds, 3 and a third. Do the wholes and the fractions separately, 2 times 1 and a half times a third, and you'll say 2 and a sixth. Short by more than a whole. Nobody'd sign for that.

Then what goes first. Parentheses, exponents, multiply and divide, add and subtract. Schools call it PEMDAS, and Patrice's nephew used to say it like a sneeze. I'll tell you where the points go. Multiply and divide are one step, taken as they come, left to right, and add and subtract are another. So: 20 minus 12 divided by 4 times 2, plus 3 squared. I'd write that big on the pad. Square first, 9. Then the middle, left to right. Twelve divided by 4 is 3, times 2 is 6. Then 20 minus 6 plus 9, twenty three. Do the times before the divide, because M comes before D in the word, and you get 12 over 8 and wind up at 27 and a half. I've seen that answer in the choices more than once. The word's for remembering. It was never the rule.
Try one. Five sixths minus one fourth. Get both bottoms to twelfths, and you should land on seven twelfths.
How the exam asks it. If you add to a fraction and the answer comes out smaller than where you started, something went sideways. Look before you pick.

Four words for a list of numbers, and the test likes all four. Take six numbers, the hours I flew six weeks running one spring: 9, 4, 12, 6, 11, 6. The mean is the plain average. Add them up, 48, and divide by how many there are, 6, and you get 8.

Median. Sort them first, smallest to biggest: 4, 6, 6, 9, 11, 12. I write the sorted list out every time, even when I'm sure I can see it, because I've been sure before. With an odd count the median's the one in the middle. With an even count, like this one, two numbers share the middle, and the median's halfway between them. Six and 9, so 7 and a half. Mode's whichever shows up most, and that's 6. Range is biggest less smallest, 12 less 4, so 8.

The miss is taking the middle before you sort. In the order I read them to you, the middle two were 12 and 6, which gives you 9, and 9 isn't anything. It's a number that wandered in. Sort first, every time. And know that a mean moves when one big number shows up. Swap the 12 for a 60 and the mean jumps to 16, while the median sits right where it was.
How the exam asks it. Sort the list on your paper before you go looking for a middle.
Thirty one years in dispatch, and I lived on one equation. Fuel on board is what you started with, less the burn an hour times the hours. Give me what's left and I'll give you the hours.

Before you solve anything, gather up what's alike, the way I'd sort a junk drawer. Like terms have the same letter to the same power, so 3x squared plus 4x minus x squared plus 2x is 2x squared plus 6x. An x squared and an x don't combine, any more than gallons and pounds do. To evaluate, put the number in with parentheses around it. I never skipped the parentheses in thirty years. X squared minus 2x when x is minus 3: minus 3 in parentheses, squared, is 9, and minus 2 times minus 3 is plus 6, so 15. Leave them off and you get minus 9 plus 6, which is minus 3, and it'll be sitting in the choices.

To solve, get the letter alone, and whatever you do to one side, do to the other. I'd draw a line down the middle of the page so I couldn't cheat. Take 5x minus 8 equals 2x plus 13. Knock 2x off both sides and you've got 3x minus 8 equals 13. Add the 8 back, 3x is 21, and x is 7. Then put the 7 back in, since I don't trust myself, and both sides come to 27. Five seconds. Cheapest insurance you'll ever buy.

What gets people is a minus parked in front of parentheses. Four, minus 3 times the quantity x minus 2. That minus 3 hits both things inside, and the second hit is minus times minus, which is plus. So it's 4 minus 3x plus 6. Plenty of people write minus 6 there. So did I, in 1972, and my wrong answer was sitting right there among the choices, smiling at me.

Two equations and two letters, add them or take one from the other till a letter falls out. That's elimination, and I did a lot of it with fuel and time on the back of a log. X plus 2y is 14, and x minus y is 2. Take the bottom from the top and 3y is 12. Y is 4, so x is 6. Or get one letter alone and put it into the other equation, which is substitution. X is y plus 2, so y plus 2, plus 2y, is 14, and you land in the same place.

Solving a formula for one letter is the same game with letters where the numbers were, and dispatch was nothing but formulas turned around backward. Take the fence around a rectangle, P equals 2l plus 2w, and say I want w. Take 2l off both sides: P minus 2l equals 2w. Now divide the whole side by 2, all of it. W equals the quantity P minus 2l, over 2. The miss is dividing only the piece next to it and calling it P minus l. When I wasn't sure, I'd try it on numbers I knew. A rectangle 10 by 5 has P of 30. Thirty minus 20, over 2, is 5. P minus l says 20, so that one's out.

Inequalities play by the same rules but one, and that one costs more points than the rest of this page put together. Multiply or divide by a negative and the sign turns around. Seven minus 3x is at least 19. Take off the 7, and minus 3x is at least 12. Divide by minus 3 and flip it, and x is at most minus 4. I don't trust that till I've tried a number, so try minus 5 in the first line. Seven plus 15 is 22, that's at least 19, and it holds.

Absolute value in an equation hands you two answers to check. Back to miles from the field: 10 miles out could be 10 north or 10 south. The absolute value of x minus 6 equals 10 means x minus 6 is 10 or it's minus 10. So x is 16 or minus 4. The miss is stopping at 16. And if somebody sets the bars equal to a negative number, there's no answer at all, because nobody's minus 10 miles from anywhere.
Try one. Three times the quantity x plus 4 equals 5x minus 2. You should get 7.
How the exam asks it. Put your answer back into the problem as written. On an inequality, try one number that should work and one that shouldn't.

An exponent's just a count of how many of the base go into the product. Two to the fifth is five 2s multiplied together, 32. I carried the four rules on an index card in my flight suit for a year, till the sweat got to it, and here they are off that card. Same base multiplied, add the exponents: 2 cubed times 2 to the fourth is 2 to the seventh. Same base divided, subtract them. A power raised to a power, multiply them, so x cubed, squared, is x to the sixth. And anything but zero, raised to the zero, is 1. Nobody believes that one the first time. I didn't.

People change the base on you. That 2 to the seventh turns into 4 to the seventh in a hurry, and I did it myself about once a month in 1972. A negative exponent doesn't make a thing negative. It flips it over: 5 to the minus 2 is one twenty fifth. And watch the parentheses. Minus 3 in parentheses, squared, is 9. Take them away and the square only grabs the 3, so you've got minus 9. The test writers know that one. So do I, now, the hard way.

When the letter's up in the exponent, the trick is getting both sides onto the same base. Then the exponents have to match, and you're back to plain algebra. Five to the quantity 2x minus 1 equals 125. I know 125's 5 cubed the way I know my own address, so 2x minus 1 is 3, and x is 2. The miss is dividing 125 by 5 and setting the exponent equal to 25. I've watched grown men do it. When the bases don't match, find one they both come from. Four to the x equals 8. Four's 2 squared, 8's 2 cubed, so 2x is 3, and x is three halves.

Square roots. Learn your squares up through 15 times 15, 225, until they come without thinking, same as your own phone number. When a root won't come out even, pull the biggest perfect square out of it: 72 is 36 times 2, so the root of 72 is 6 root 2. You can only add roots with the same thing inside, same as you can't add pounds to gallons and get anything you'd want to sign. Root 9 plus root 16 is 3 plus 4, 7. Patrice caught me calling that root 25 in 1981, at this table, helping her nephew with his homework, and she still tells it at Thanksgiving.

Scientific notation is for numbers too long to say out loud, and I never once said one aloud. The front number is at least 1 and less than 10, and it's multiplied by ten to some power. So 32,000 comes out 3.2 times 10 to the fourth, and 0.0061 is 6.1 times 10 to the minus third. To multiply two of them I'd do the front numbers, add the powers, and if the front came out 10 or more I'd slide the decimal a notch and bump the power, so 12 times 10 to the fifth turns into 1.2 times 10 to the sixth.
Try one, and don't let the minus scare you. Three times 10 to the minus 2, times 5 times 10 to the sixth. Kit got 1.5 times 10 to the fifth on her first go, which is right.
How the exam asks it. A negative exponent never makes the answer negative. It makes a fraction.
Factoring, the way I did it at the table.
At the nav table I factored everything I touched. A number in pieces is a number you can cancel, and the pieces went down the margin of the log.

Multiplying two binomials, every term in one shakes hands with every term in the other. X plus 6, times x minus 2: x squared, minus 2x, plus 6x, minus 12. The middle two make 4x, so it's x squared plus 4x minus 12. Skip the handshakes in the middle and you'll pick the wrong one, which is what the wrong one's there for. X plus 5, squared, is x squared plus 10x plus 25, and every year somebody writes x squared plus 25.

Factoring flies it backward. Pull out anything every term shares first, so 4x squared plus 10x is 2x times the quantity 2x plus 5. Then hunt two numbers that multiply to the last number and add to the middle. That's my margin. For x squared minus 9x plus 20, I'd write 1 and 20, 2 and 10, 4 and 5. Four and 5 make 9, both take the minus, and it's x minus 4 times x minus 5.

Two you should know on sight. X squared minus 49 is a difference of squares, x plus 7 times x minus 7. X squared plus 49 won't factor with ordinary numbers at all, and if a choice says it does, it's lying to you. And if none of the choices looks fully factored, don't panic. Multiply each choice back out and pick the one that matches what you were handed.

Letters in a fraction simplify the way numbers do. Factor the top, factor the bottom, and cancel what they share. I'd say it to myself every time: factors cancel, terms don't. A factor's multiplied, a term's added. X squared minus 9, over x squared plus 5x plus 6. Top's x plus 3 times x minus 3. Bottom's x plus 2 times x plus 3. Strike the x plus 3s and you've got x minus 3 over x plus 2. The miss is striking the two x squareds, and you can't, because each one's added to something. One more thing. X can't be minus 2 or minus 3 to start with, since either one puts a zero on the bottom.

A quadratic's got an x squared in it, and usually two answers. Zero on one side first, every time. X squared minus x equals 30 turns into x squared minus x minus 30 equals zero. My margin says 5 and 6, one apart, the 6 takes the minus, and x is 6 or minus 5. Try to factor with the 30 still sitting over on the right and you'll get a mess for your trouble. I've made that mess. If it's a width or a length, the negative one's no good to anybody.

Some won't factor. For those there's the quadratic formula, minus b, plus or minus the root of b squared minus 4ac, all over 2a, and I never once used it in an airplane. Mostly I'd look under the root. If that came out positive I had two answers, zero gave me one, and negative meant there wasn't a real one to find.
Try one. X squared plus x minus 42 equals zero. The pair is 6 and 7, and you should land on 6 or minus 7.
How the exam asks it. Zero on one side first, then factor. Then put each answer back in.

Ninety degrees is the square corner, and I'd find it first on anything you hand me. Less is acute, more up to 180 is obtuse, and 180 is a straight line. Angles that make 90 are complementary, and ones that make 180 are supplementary. I kept them straight by the alphabet, C before S and 90 before 180. Where two lines cross, the angles across from each other are equal, and they're called vertical angles. I just called them twins. A line across two parallel ones makes eight angles in two sizes, and the two sizes make 180. If it crosses them square, all eight are 90.

A triangle's angles make 180 whatever shape it's in, and I've never met one that cheated. Isosceles has two equal sides and two equal angles across from them. Equilateral is 60 all around. Scalene has no two sides the same. And the biggest angle sits across from the longest side.

In a right triangle, the two legs squared add up to the long side squared. That long side's the hypotenuse, across from the square corner. Legs of 8 and 15: 64 and 225 make 289, and the root is 17. Handed the long side, I subtract instead. Long side 25 and a leg of 7 leaves 576, so the other leg is 24. I flew with a copilot who added the legs straight across in his head and told the pilot we'd be early. We weren't.
Learn the families. 3, 4, 5. 5, 12, 13. 8, 15, 17. 7, 24, 25. They were on that same index card. Any of them multiplied up counts, and when two numbers fit a family you've got the third for free.
Five hundred, a hundred forty, four eighty. That's seven, twenty four, twenty five, times twenty. I worked it over Iowa with the Doppler dead and the pilot asking me every two minutes.

The 45, 45, 90 is a square cut corner to corner, so the legs match and the long side is a leg times root 2. The 30, 60, 90 is what you get sawing an equilateral triangle down the middle. Short leg x, long side 2x, the other leg x root 3. Long side 12, legs 6 and 6 root 3. Folks hang the root 3 on the long side. I did it the first week of nav school, and the instructor wrote NO across my paper in red, about four inches high.

Similar triangles are the same shape in two sizes. Angles match, and every pair of matching sides scales by one number. You can get the height of anything that throws a shadow that way. A 6 foot man throws a 4 foot shadow, and at the same hour a mast throws one 30 feet long. Six over 4 equals the mast over 30, so the mast's 45 feet. The miss is adding. The mast's shadow is 26 feet longer, so somebody adds 26 to the 6 and says 32. I'd tell him similar means times, never plus. Charts work the same. On one of mine an inch was ten nautical miles, so three and a half inches was thirty five, and I measured a lot of inches.
Try one. Legs of 9 and 40. It's another family, and the hypotenuse is 41.
How the exam asks it. I find the square corner before I touch a number. Whatever's across from it is the long side, every time.

Straight sided shapes, I take two off the number of sides and multiply by 180, and that's every inside angle added up. A pentagon's 540, and a regular one is 108 a corner. The outside angles of anything add to 360, which I could do in my sleep and probably did. Forget the take two and you'll get 900 for a pentagon, which is more corner than any pentagon ever had.
I drew more circles on charts than anything else, range rings mostly. Every one of them was a radius somebody handed me.

Circles next. Center to edge is the radius, and straight across is the diameter, twice as long. I used to tell new navigators the radius is the one you square and the diameter is the one you get handed. Around is 2 pi r. Inside is pi r squared. Hand me a diameter of 14 and I'd halve it before I did one other thing: radius 7, around 14 pi, call it 44, and inside 49 pi, call it 154.

Three more names and you can have your coffee. A chord, first. Two dots on the rim, a ruler between them, done. The longest chord there is runs through the middle, and you already know its name, the diameter. An arc is the rim between those two dots, the bent part, and it goes by its angle the way a slice does. Say the radius is 8. Around is 16 pi, and a 90 degree arc is a quarter of that, 4 pi. Somebody always says 16 pi there, and that's the slice's area, not the arc. Then tangent. It touches once and leaves. Where it touches, the radius meets it square. Square corner, right triangle, and you know what to do with those.

Her first night at it, Kit squared the diameter instead of the radius before she caught it. Pi times 14 squared is 196 pi, four times too big, and test writers love that number. The other miss is answering how far around when they asked how much inside, and I've done that one at two in the morning over Nebraska.
Slices go by the angle. I'd cut it by the turn, not by eye. A 120 degree slice is a third of the way around, so a third of the area, and with radius 3 that's 3 pi.

Inscribed means drawn inside and touching. I picture a coffee can in a box that fits it snug: the can's width is the box's side. So a square 6 on a side holds a circle of radius 3, and the four corners left over come to 36 minus 9 pi. Now turn it around. Put a square inside a circle with its corners on the rim, and it's the square's diagonal that runs across the circle. Radius 5, diagonal 10. A square's area is its diagonal squared, halved, so 100 over 2, 50. Call the 10 a side and you'll say 100. I'd have said it too, once.
Try one. A regular decagon has ten sides. One inside angle is 144 degrees.
How the exam asks it. Handed a diameter, I halve it before I square anything. Always.

Perimeter's the fence, area's the lawn, in square units. Rectangle, length times width. Half the base times the height for a triangle, and the height hangs straight down from the top corner, never along the slant. Kit asked me why. I told her to tie a nut to a thread and hang it off the corner, and she did it right there at the yellow table with one of Patrice's spools. A trapezoid's the odd duck. Average its two parallel sides, then times the height.

Volume's in cubic units. A box is length times width times height. A cylinder is pi r squared times how far it runs, standing up or lying on its side, and I've never seen a tank care which. Surface area is the paint: a 4 by 5 by 6 box holds 120 and takes 148 square units to cover.
Then scale. Blow a shape up three times in every direction and its area goes up nine times, its volume twenty seven. Lengths go by the scale, area by its square, volume by its cube.
How the exam asks it. Square units for area, cubic units for volume. Say the units out loud and the wrong ones sound wrong.

Points go x first, then y. Across the hall, then up the stairs, and I've said that to every student I ever had. Slope's how steep the line runs. Rise over run. From 1, minus 2 to 5, 6: y climbs 8, x goes 4. Slope 2.

There are two ways to blow it, and I've done both. Flip it, run over rise, and you get one half. Or take the y's in one order and the x's in the other, and the sign comes out backward. Whatever point you put first on top, put it first on the bottom. Uphill to the right, positive. Downhill, negative. Flat, zero. A wall's slope is undefined, because the run's zero and nothing divides by zero, not even for me.

Written y equals m x plus b, the m's your slope and the b's where it crosses the y axis. Hand me 2x plus y equals 7 and I'd get y alone first, the way you'd clear the table before you spread a chart: y equals minus 2x plus 7. Parallel lines share a slope. Perpendicular ones flip it and change the sign, 2 against minus a half.

Distance between two points is the right triangle all over again. I can't get away from that triangle, and now neither can you. From 1, 1 to 4, 5 is 3 across and 4 up, so 5. The midpoint's just the two averages, add and halve, once for the x's and once for the y's.
Try one. The line from minus 2, 1 to 2, 3. The slope is one half.
How the exam asks it. I write the two points one over the other, the way I'd stack two fixes on a log, and subtract straight down.

The furnace kicked on. Over the table, on the fridge whiteboard, Saturday, April 3, two weeks out, was boxed in green: PRACTICE TEST, 5 HRS, ME ON THE CLOCK. Under that, small, in his black marker, 2019.

Heading and track she knew the way she knew the jet, from outside it. She'd watched a thousand of them go from the cab of her truck at the edge of the ramp, coffee going cold on the dash. Vern had done this one with half his panel dead, at four hundred some knots, and a grease pencil. She dug a sheet of Graham's graph paper out of the junk drawer, under the takeout menus. Course, straight up the page. Wind, square across from the left, 140. The 500 was the airplane through the air, wherever he'd had it pointed.
The wind is square across the course. Where did Vern's 480 come from?
A. Take the 140 off the 500 and call the 360 his.
B. Call it a little under 500, and leave the rest for Tuesday.
C. Square both, take the wind's square off, and find the root.
D. Square both, add the two, and take the root of all of it.

She put the 500 on the long side, across from the square corner. That was the airplane's own arrow, the one doing the work, and the wind just leaned on it. The wind was a short side. Whatever was left over was the ground. Five hundred squared, 250,000. One forty squared, 19,600. The difference was 230,400, and she worked the root down by guessing: 480. Then she saw it, a little late. Seven times twenty, twenty four times twenty, twenty five times twenty. He hadn't squared a thing. She folded the log back along its crease.

That'll hold, Sergeant. When the wind's square across your course, your own airspeed is the long side, the hypotenuse, across from the right angle. I always drew it before I did a thing, because the drawing tells you which side's which. Wind on one leg, ground speed on the other. Square the long side, take the wind's square off, and find the root. The test's the same deal: find the square corner first. And look for a family. Seven, twenty four, twenty five saved me a lot of squaring in that airplane.

Tuesday at seven the index card was where she'd left it two weeks back, against the percolator, and neither of them said anything about it. Vern didn't mention the Saturday log. She didn't either. It was in her coat on the hook, on top of the other sheet.
He'd seen her graph paper, though, folded in with her homework, the triangle and its three numbers and her arithmetic down the side. He looked at it a while and didn't mark it.
Same airplane. Same wind, two seven zero at one forty. He drew a line straight down a fresh page of the legal pad. Only now you're southbound. Which way does the nose go, Sergeant, and about how far?
A. Straight down 180, and let it drift.
B. To the left of the track, around 164.
C. Right of the track, about 196.
D. To the right of the track, around 208.

The wind came from the west. Southbound, west was on her right. Point a little into it and it would push her back onto the line. Sixteen degrees, same triangle, only the other side of the course: 180 plus 16. She wrote 196. Vern turned the pad around so it faced him and nodded at it. Steer one ninety six, make good one eighty.

Right. Log it. Winds get named for where they come from, so two seven zero is a west wind. You lean the nose a little into it and let it push you back onto your line. Heading is where the nose points. Track is where you actually go. The gap between them is your wind correction angle. For a quick look we used the rule of sixty: crosswind times sixty, over true airspeed. A hundred forty times sixty over five hundred comes out about seventeen. The triangle says sixteen. I'd start my turn on seventeen and fix it later.
After that he put four sets on the table, typed, stapled at the corner. MATH KNOWLEDGE, twenty five apiece. Algebra mostly, then circles and triangles toward the back of each one.

The real one's twenty five of these in twenty two minutes. That's not quite a minute each. He set the egg timer next to the stack and took his hand off it. Practice test is a week from Saturday. How you run these between now and then is yours.
Four sets, and a week and a half to the practice test. How should Kit run them?
A. Work every set untimed till each answer's right, and save the clock for Saturday.
B. Run each set at eleven minutes, half the clock, to build speed.
C. Skip the kinds she already knows, and drill only the factoring.
D. Set the egg timer to twenty two for each set, then rework her misses slowly.

She cranked it to twenty two and went. The algebra went fast. The circles didn't. Twice she put a diameter in where the radius went, and at the bell she was guessing on the last one. Twenty one right. Then she did the four misses over with no clock at all, slowly, and found both diameters in about a minute. Now you know where your time goes, Vern said.

That's the fix I'd have taken. Run it under the real clock, then go back over the misses with no clock. The timed run shows you where the minutes go and what you do when they run out. The slow pass afterward fixes what broke. Accuracy first, then pace on top of it. That's the order for every timed block on this test.
Decision four. Pairs down the margin.
At half past eight he took the pencil from behind his ear and wrote across the top of a clean page.

Spring of ninety nine, the controllers moved our refueling block on us while we were in it. New one was ten miles longer than it was wide, two thousand square miles of sky, and nobody on the radio would tell me the width. There wasn't a thing in that airplane that would do it for me.
Under it, in his capitals: W TIMES THE QUANTITY W PLUS 10 EQUALS 2,000. Factor it the way I did.
The block is ten miles longer than it is wide and covers 2,000 square miles. How wide is it?
A. Forty miles wide, and fifty long.
B. Twenty miles wide and a hundred long.
C. Forty wide, or minus fifty, and keep both.
D. Close to forty five, the root of two thousand.

She wrote it out the long way first: W squared plus 10W minus 2,000 equals zero. Then she did it his way, the pairs of 2,000 down the margin, 1 and 2,000, 2 and 1,000, 4 and 500, on down, until two of them were ten apart. Forty and fifty. W plus 50, times W minus 40. Forty, or minus fifty, and nobody flies a block of sky minus fifty miles wide. Pairs down the margin, Vern said. Took me about as long as it took you.

That'll hold, Sergeant. Get zero on one side, then hunt for two numbers that multiply to the constant and land on the middle term. Pairs of 2,000, one plus and one minus, ten apart: fifty and forty. Then make the problem pick. A width can't be negative, so it's forty. That's the whole method, and it's most of the factoring on this subtest.
Decision five. Thirty one and three quarters.
Thursday she was on days. Gene had left a note clipped to the board by the door, in his square printing: STICK THE GENSET TANK. ORDER IF UNDER HALF. G.

The plant's backup generator lived in its own shed behind the high service building, a diesel the size of a pickup that ran the pumps when the power went. Its fuel was in a steel tank on cradles beside it, a long cylinder lying on its side, painted gray. She dropped the wooden stick through the fill cap until it touched bottom and pulled it up. Wet to thirty one and three quarter inches.
The chart for it was taped inside the shed door, laminated, gone yellow. The laminate had torn off above the 30 row and under the 33 years ago, and nobody had printed another.

Depth in inches down the side, from thirty to thirty three. Quarter inches across the top. Thirty inches: six sixty seven, six seventy five, six eighty two, six eighty nine. Thirty one: six ninety seven, seven oh four, seven twelve, seven nineteen. Thirty two: seven twenty seven, seven thirty four, seven forty one, seven forty nine. Thirty three: seven fifty six, seven sixty four, seven seventy one, seven seventy nine.
The stick reads 31 and three quarters. What does the chart say?
A. 712 gallons, in row 31, the half inch column.
B. 719 gallons, in row 31, three quarter column.
C. 749 gallons, in row 32, the three quarter column.
D. 689 gallons, row 30, three quarter column.

Finger on 31, slide across to the three quarters: 719. Then the neighbors, the way she'd started doing on Vern's tables. 712 before it, 749 right under it, 689 right over it. Then the problem. Under half of what? Nobody had written full down anywhere. The only other thing on paper was a plate riveted to the tank: 6 FT DIA X 8 FT.

Right. Log it. Row, then column, then a look at what's around it. That habit is what Table Reading pays for. The neighbors of the right cell are exactly where a slip lands you, and the choices on the test often sit there.
There wasn't a clean sheet of paper in that shed, so she flipped the chart over and used the back, with the pencil that hung off the stick hook on a bootlace.

A drum lying down, really, just a big one. Six feet across and eight end to end, by the plate. Gene wanted half, and in twenty years nobody had worked out what full was. Out the shed door the river was up and brown, carrying half a tree past the intake, and she thought about Yates down there some night soon with his flashlight, cussing at it.
It's six feet across and eight long. How much does the full tank hold, in cubic feet?
A. 24 pi, three times pi times eight.
B. 72 pi: 3 squared, times pi, times 8.
C. 288 pi, squaring the whole six feet.
D. 48 pi, the six around times the eight.

Radius three. Pi times nine times eight, 72 pi. Pi's a little over three, so call it 226 cubic feet. There's 7.48 gallons in a cubic foot, which she knew as well as she knew 8.34, and that made it about 1,692 gallons full, and 846 at half. The stick said 719. She called the fuel dealer from the shed and ordered 950 gallons, a little under what would top it off, and wrote the math on Gene's note under his initial.

That's the fix I'd have taken. A tank lying on its side is a cylinder, and a cylinder is the round end times the length. Round end, pi r squared. The radius is half of six, three. So 9 pi times 8, 72 pi cubic feet. Halve the diameter before anything gets squared. Then the units tell you you're done, cubic feet for a volume.
Saturday morning she took set three to the heritage room. Vern was there on Saturdays, and it was quiet, and nobody but Vern ever came in.

At ten Corbin Haas came in. Jeans, a ball cap, a shoebox under his arm. In the shoebox was the altimeter that had sat on his shelf in February with a yellow tag on it. It had come out of Vern's display case at Christmas, and he'd been at it on his own time since, nights, after the shop cleared out. The needles moved now. He set it on the glass. Don't let anybody tap it. It's older than me. Vern went to the back to find the key to the case, and took his time looking.
Corbin looked at her sheets on the table, the circles and triangles and the egg timer sitting on top of them like a paperweight.

First week, they don't let you near an airplane. It's a classroom and a stack of books, and every one of those books is written from the inside. What's the airplane doing, what do your hands do about it. You know two two eight better than anybody on that ramp. You know it from the outside. You'll walk around it in your head when you ought to be flying it. He tapped the shoebox lid twice, the way you'd knock on a panel to hear if it was loose. The ones who flew in college already think like the airplane. I thought like the guy with the flashlight. Took me a month to quit, and I didn't have a month.

He put his hands in his pockets and looked at the altimeter instead of at her. I called my mom every Sunday night down there. Week five she heard it from a lady at church. I'd talked to her the night before and said fine. He let that sit. So when it quits going fine for you, Darrow, who hears it from you first?
A. Tell him she'll handle it herself, the way she always has.
B. Tell him it'll go fine, she's older and knows the jet.
C. Tell him Graham first, then him, if he'll pick up.
D. Tell him about 2019, right there by the display case.

Graham first. Then you, if you'll pick up. Corbin looked at her a long time, long enough that she thought she'd gotten it wrong. Nobody's asked me for anything but the story in two years. He took her pencil and wrote a phone number across the top of set three, over problem one, and gave the pencil back. I'll pick up.

That'll hold, Sergeant. Communication, and a little Mentoring running the other way. You named who you'd tell before there was anything to tell, and you asked him straight for something only he can give. That's the shape the test rewards: raise trouble early, directly, with the right people, before it's a crisis. Asking for help is part of doing the job. It isn't a failure of it.

Corbin left a little before eleven. Vern came back with the key just after, which she figured was not an accident, and set the altimeter in the case beside the attitude indicator under the glass. The needles sat at field elevation and stayed there. Vern stood over them with his hands behind his back.
He'd been gone the better part of an hour. The key ring had been on his belt the whole time. She'd seen it when he walked back in.
Vern took a long time finding that key. What does Kit say to him about it?
A. Ask him what he'd tell Graham, if he were in her shoes.
B. Thank him for the hour, and leave his reasons with him.
C. Ask him straight out whether he set the morning up.
D. Say nothing about it, and go back to problem fourteen.

Thanks for the hour. Vern locked the case and put the key in his shirt pocket. Sergeant Haas has been after me since Christmas to take that thing back. He sat down and pulled set three over to problem fourteen, and that was all either of them said about it.

Right. Log it. Communication. Somebody did you a kindness without making a thing of it, so you name it plainly, once, and you don't make him explain it. Thanks, then back to work. On the test, the best answer to a favor is usually the short, direct thank you to the person, not a question about his motives and not silence.
Decision nine. Too heavy to land.
By the next Tuesday she'd run sets two and three on the egg timer, twenty two minutes each, and reworked the misses slow. Twenty two right, then twenty three. The circles had quit getting her.
Vern didn't spend long on it. He turned the legal pad sideways and printed: W EQUALS 255,000 MINUS 10,000 T.

From my dispatch years. A freighter out of Kansas City turned back twenty minutes out with a hydraulic light, and that model had no way to dump fuel. It was too heavy to put down. W is its weight in pounds after T hours of circling, and the landing limit was two thirty. Under the equation he wrote: W IS AT MOST 230,000.
How long does the freighter have to hold before it can land?
A. At least forty eight and a half hours.
B. No more than two and a half hours.
C. At least twenty three hours.
D. At least two and a half hours.

255,000 minus 10,000 T, at most 230,000. Take the 255,000 over: minus 10,000 T is at most minus 25,000. Divide by minus 10,000 and flip it. T is at least 2.5. Two and a half hours over the river in a holding pattern, Vern said, and the captain called me every one of them. I had another captain once who thought the flip was a suggestion.

That's the fix I'd have taken. An inequality solves like an equation, with one rule on top. Divide or multiply by a negative and the sign turns around. Here the minus 10,000 does it, and at most becomes at least. Then check it against sense. The longer it circles, the lighter it gets, so the answer has to be a least.
Wednesday, a quarter to five, between the plant and supper. Her phone buzzed on the truck seat.
A text from Fisk. Sgt Darrow. Boyd says you're doing my torque retrain at April drill. I've got the study card. Can you look at it before? Don't want to blow it in front of everybody.
She read it at the stop sign by the grain elevator. It was the most words he'd ever put in one text.
Fisk wants help before April drill. What should Kit tell him?
A. Give him a time this week, and make him walk her through it.
B. Send him a photo of her own card, with every step filled in.
C. Tell him Boyd's the one to ask about all of that now.
D. Tell him to bring it to drill, and they'll go over it there.

She texted back from the stop sign. Thursday, four, the Riverside. Bring the card. You talk. Thursday he was in the back booth in his warehouse shirt with the card face down on the table. She asked questions and didn't answer any. He had the steps in the wrong order once and found it himself, before she said a word, and went red, and went back and did it right. When he was done he looked at her. You didn't tell me a single thing. She paid for his pie. She was halfway home before she noticed she'd done it Vern's way, ask and wait, without deciding to.

That'll hold, Sergeant. Mentoring. A time, a place where nobody's watching, and him doing the work while you ask. You didn't hand him answers, you didn't pass him off, and you didn't save it for the shop floor. The test leans the same way. Develop people by making them do it, privately, soon.
Decision eleven. Carts on the bench.

Thursday night, April 1, Graham had a stack of sophomore lab reports and his red pen. Carts let go off a ramp and rolling down the long level bench, distance against time, every graph a little different from the next one.
He slid one across to her without looking up. Two points marked on a straight line, seconds across the bottom, centimeters up the side. The student had written 1/15 at the bottom for the speed.
You've got Saturday on your mind. Do one for me anyway. What should it say?
Behind him on the whiteboard, under Saturday's green box, was the 2019 he'd written. Neither of them had looked at it all week, which in that kitchen took some doing.
The sophomore's two dots sit at 30 centimeters after 2 seconds and 90 after 6. What's the slope of that line?
A. Fifteen: 90 over 6, from the last point alone.
B. Twenty two and a half: 90 over 4.
C. One fifteenth: four across over sixty up.
D. Fifteen: sixty up over four across.

She took the two points the long way, the way Vern would have. Ninety less thirty, sixty. Six less two, four. Fifteen centimeters a second, and the student had it upside down. Graham wrote it on the paper in red and drew a little arrow at the line. That's what I keep telling them. The slope's the speed. She nodded. He went back to the stack.

Right. Log it. Up 60, over 4, slope 15. On a distance and time graph that's the speed, so it carries units, centimeters a second here. Graham tells his sophomores the same thing. Subtract both points in the same order and the sign looks after itself.

Friday night the whiteboard came off the fridge again. It slid off its bracket while Graham was writing 8:00 into Saturday's box, and the marker went down the whole week in one long green line. He laughed at it. Bracket. Again. He pinned it to the fridge with his palm, still grinning. Eight o'clock. I'll call time at the end of every block, and I won't say anything else.
She went out for the drill. The light in the garage came on by itself when she opened the side door, the way it always did.

The drill was on the pegboard. Its battery wasn't. She tried behind the mower. Graham had pulled the mower out on Sunday for the first cut of the year and shoved it back in crooked, and one corner of the blue tarp had come up with the handle.
Under the corner was a rail. Pale wood, worn smooth, with round spindles under it, close together.

She lifted the tarp. A crib. Maple, from the color, with the mattress board bare and a paper tag tied to one post with string. SOLD, in grease pencil, and a date. April 2025. Two springs ago. The KC-46 talk had just started that spring, and he'd stood at this same door and asked her whether this could be the year, and she'd said after.

She put her hand on the rail. Somebody else's hands had rubbed it pale long before it ever got here. Graham's whiteboard stopped at May, at its aluminum edge. She'd seen that in February and hadn't asked, and now she knew what he'd kept off it.
She put the tarp back. She put it back the way it had been, the corner under the mower handle, and that took longer than it should have.
She'd given him Saturday herself, all of 2019 with the paper on the table. And he'd had this out here two springs, under a tarp, and never once asked her to come and look.
The tarp is back over it. What will Kit do about it tonight?
A. Leave it, and give him hers before she asks for his.
B. Go back in and ask him what's under it, tonight.
C. Let it stay something she never saw, from now on.
D. Call her mother and ask what Graham's said.
She left it. His was his. Hers came first, and it was seven years overdue, and she wasn't going to ask him for anything until she'd set it down in front of him. After that, the tarp was his to lift.

That's the fix I'd have taken. Integrity, and the order it comes in. You don't ask somebody for their truth while you're sitting on yours. Direct and private is still how it gets done. In this case hers goes first, tomorrow night, and then his. On the test the best answer is usually the direct one, done soon, and here it's still direct and still soon. It just starts with her.
The battery was in the jar of screws on the shelf, same as February, under a handful of drywall anchors nobody in this house had ever used. She stood there holding it.

Tomorrow night, then. Kitchen table, the sheet out of her coat, and hers said first, all of it, before anybody touched that tarp. She had the battery so tight in her fist the edge was biting her. In the kitchen Graham would still be holding the whiteboard to the fridge with one hand, reading Saturday off it, waiting on her and the drill.

Graham had put that light up himself, the summer they bought the place, and set it on two minutes because one wasn't enough to find your keys. Two minutes went by. Nothing in the garage moved, so it clicked off on her.
